wording: P59 treats loyalty as a practical disposition to persist in an intrinsically valued association, an executive virtue whose worth depends on its object. On Hirschman's account it should be given until it becomes clear that the institution cannot be recuperated, and loyalty to a particular object is forfeited when the object shows itself no longer worthy or capable of being a source of associational satisfaction or identity, though the breakpoint differs between people (P59's example of a spouse's infidelity). A loyal opposition stays within bounds compatible with the object's flourishing; whistle blowing should be a last resort, for serious wrongdoing, well grounded and likely to be effective. On religious roots P59 notes only that Old Testament writers framed fickleness as (un)faithfulness and that Confucian thought has long engaged loyalty.
